Academic conferences

Strategy Science · AOM · OUI · SMS

How many academic conferences have you attended?

  1. A0–2
  2. B3–5
  3. C6–10
  4. D10+

How much do we need conferences?

An open question.

What can a conference give you?

Do different kinds of conferences matter?

Conferences I have been to

Who is there

Everyone comes with a purpose

  • networking up
  • meeting coauthors
  • bonding with groups
  • gaining visibility

You only get what you put in. Going without an aim is not worth much.

Benefit: a reason to finish and to practise

Deadlines

  • A yearly deadline gets you to submit
  • AOM and SMS: you can review papers
  • Rare for students

Presenting

  • A skill that takes practice
  • Watch strong presentations
  • Learn from them and copy what works

Benefit: finding your room

Which room do you belong to?

  • AOM and SMS have many rooms
  • Early on: follow general interest
  • Organic, spontaneous
  • Where do you focus?
  • Whose people do you want to meet?
  • Match faces to surnames you read

My rooms

  • Open source, user innovation
  • A bit of platforms, a bit of geopolitics
  • AI is everywhere

Benefit: people

Peers

  • Students at stronger schools
  • Similar interests
  • A year ahead of you
  • Young APs you share ties with
  • Let them lead the way

Core people

  • The pillars of your field
  • The gatekeepers
  • No need to force it

Beyond “say hi”

  • Present your work
  • Draw like-minded people
  • Get senior feedback
  • Ask good questions
  • Visible in small circles

First time strangers, second time friends

  • Over the years: a cohort, a support group, coauthors

Benefit: ideas and feedback

Why luck

  • A 15–20 minute talk rarely gets real feedback
  • PDWs help more: papers go in ahead
  • Everyone reads and comments on each other’s papers

Cost: time and money

A fixed research budget

Visa and immigration: cost and risk

Preparing, plus research time and classes you miss

The opportunity cost is real.

Cost: overexposure

Your ideas

  • Ideas not thought through
  • Papers not ready
  • Bigger conference, bigger risk of being scooped

Yourself

  • The audience may be your future hiring committee
  • Bad first impression: work, presentation style, offline talk
  • Can be worse than not showing up

The other side

  • A good first impression
  • Visibility over the years as you improve
  • A network for the job market and letters

Tricky.
I’m still exploring, learning, and making mistakes.

My favourites: the smaller, the better

OUI

Harvard Business School · Jul 2026

  • My research interests
  • People close to my work
  • Some conversations already deep

Strategy Science

Boulder · May 2026

  • The field’s most active, productive researchers
  • The newest work
  • Hosting it: many papers elsewhere repeat SS

AOM

Philadelphia · Aug 2026

  • Everyone goes: find your people
  • Connect privately
  • PDWs and symposia ≫ paper sessions

SMS

Berlin · Oct 2026

  • Shared coffee, lunch, dinner
  • Not days of running between rooms
  • Common Ground: one big table

Construct Laplace

Every tested hypothesis in strategy and organization research, in one place

What it is

Click the image to open the walkthrough on YouTube: youtu.be/ybqCSSAOUnk

A searchable record of the hypotheses that strategy and organization research has stated and tested.

4,784papers, 1959 to 2026
24,526hypotheses, each as printed
2,052constructs in one dictionary

How it is built

How to use it

Example question to an AI assistant

“How do studies measure patent quality when forward citations are not available?”

The assistant found 236 measures in 153 papers and grouped them into 14 families, such as claim counts, family size and novelty, each with its papers.

Worked example, technical appendix §11.5
